body: I'm not entirely sure that this would make sense in the general case. If we could infer that the left hand side of the assignment is an object generated by a call to that `__new__` then we could assume this is good enough and we are mutating the same object. But unless we can do that, ignoring by default messages emitted in `__new__` sounds a bit artificial, since some of them might be still valid (e.g one can use a different object to fetch a private attribute)

> e.g one can use a different object to fetch a private attribute

I agree. Did not think of that one.

In the worst case, I think it is acceptable to append `# pylint: disable=<xyz>` to the violating line. This is in any case which should not happen *often*. If the implementation of this detection turns out to be a huge can of worms this could be seen as "not worth the effort" ;)

I'm having the same problem with the equal operator.
object.__eq__(self, other)
Is this the same case?
In case of Python 3 if I try object.__eq__(self, other: 'TypeHint') still complains.

I agree with you @limdor. 
@PCManticore what do you think about it?
@hippo91 and @limdor Yes, this sounds like something that we can fix for single underscore attributes that are accessed in dunder methods.

body:
> What about private variables of other instances of the same class?

This feels a bit more controversial to me. When marking a variable as "private", you normally want to say that *no* external actor should be able to modify (or access) it. Think of two instances of `Car` for example. Should one instance be allowed to start the engine of the other?

If you expect that the attribute is accessed from the outside, then it might actually not be a good candidate for a "private" attribute.

My initial post was triggered by the `__new__` function, which is a bit special.
